transcript:
Meeting header: Recorded at 2027-03-11T16:00:00-07:00, Duration ~47 minutes
Attendees: Alex Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (Orion CTO), Liam Chen (Orion ML), Evan Park (Orion Security), Sofia Rivera (Orion Product)

Summary: AE + SE demo of Redwood's structured output / JSON-mode and function/tool-calling capabilities. Focus on schema validation/guardrails, streaming JSON output, tool calling hooks, Console examples (Optimize recommendations), and deployment discussion (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private/VPC) with security Qs.

Topics: structured output, JSON schema enforcement, function calling, tool calling, guardrails, streaming vs buffered output, performance/latency tradeoffs, SOC2/KMS, Dedicated capacity vs Hosted, pilot/POC scope.

00:00 Alex Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood, with Priya who is our solutions engineer. Quick confirm of time, we have about 45 minutes, is that still good?
00:12 Maya Thompson: Yes that's good, thanks. We're excited to see the structured output bit - we saw the email.
00:18 Alex Carter: Awesome. Quick agenda: we'll show JSON-mode and schema validation in the API, demo function calling / tool calling flows, then jump into the Console and Optimize recommendations for cost/latency, and end with next steps.
00:32 Priya Shah: I'll kick off with a short live demo. Note: the transcription might miss a couple of proper nouns, sorry in advance, but i'll keep callouts on the screen.
00:43 Priya Shah: Ok, first example - we send a prompt like: "Extract invoice metadata: date, vendor, total, line_items as JSON" and pin a JSON schema. Our API has a JSON mode where you send a schema and the model attempts to emit only valid JSON that matches the schema.
00:58 Priya Shah: (typing sounds) Here you can see the schema: required fields invoice_id, vendor.name, total.amount, currency, line_items array with quantity, sku, description.
01:12 Liam Chen: Quick q - how strict is the enforcement? Will it always be valid JSON or do we get partials?
01:20 Priya Shah: Great question. It's probabilistic - model tries to match the schema, and we add a lightweight validator on the service side. If the output fails validation we can re-call with a repair prompt automatically, or we can return a structured error with the model's raw text. For high-sensitivity flows we recommend schema + server-side validation and a short repair loop, which we demo here.
01:40 Priya Shah: (runs demo) See the first response - it had a missing currency field. The runtime detected the schema mismatch and automatically re-issued a constrained prompt, then returned valid JSON. The Console will show the validation error trace.
01:58 Evan Park: Do you log the raw model output? For compliance we need auditability, but only if we can control retention.
02:07 Alex Carter: Yes, by default we capture both the model-generated text and the final validated payload in audit logs; retention is configurable - part of the Dedicated/Private offering we can change retention to meet policy. We integrate with customer KMS for envelope encryption.
02:24 Evan Park: KMS details? Bring your own?
02:27 Alex Carter: We support BYOK with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and common HSMs for Private. For Hosted we manage keys but can rotate. We'll include the SOC2/ISO docs and a KMS note in the follow-up.
02:40 Priya Shah: Back to the demo - next, function calling. Instead of returning final JSON, you can map outputs to function calls. For example, we show a tool integration: postInvoice(api) that accepts an object matching the invoice schema. The model will either return a function call payload or direct JSON when confirmed.
03:03 Priya Shah: (demo) Here the model decides to call postInvoice. Redwood's runtime serializes the arguments into a sanitized payload and optionally executes the customer-registered tool webhook. We include a dry-run mode where we only show the call arguments in the Console so you can review before execution.
03:21 Maya Thompson: If it calls the webhook, what's the retry policy? We prefer idempotent retries.
03:27 Priya Shah: We recommend idempotency keys in the tool API. Redwood does automatic retry with exponential backoff for transient failures, and you can set max retries per route. Also configurable: at-most-once vs at-least-once semantics based on route policy.
03:44 Liam Chen: How do you handle streaming JSON when using function calls? Streaming partial object pieces seems risky.
03:49 Priya Shah: Good point. For structured outputs we typically buffer until a valid JSON chunk is produced, but we support streaming tokens for cases where latency matters and the consumer can handle incremental JSON tokens. The Console shows an example where streaming is enabled and the UI assembles the object, validating as chunks arrive.
04:15 Priya Shah: Now I want to demo guardrails - we have schema-level guards and policy-level guards. Schema prevents malformed shapes. Policy guards can block certain sensitive fields (PII) or enforce redaction. You can attach pattern validators or custom JS validators in the Private deployment.
04:36 Evan Park: Can we add a rule to strip social-security-number patterns and route those to a secure vault?
04:42 Priya Shah: Yes, you can detect patterns with a pre-processor and route to a vault or redact. In Dedicated/Private we can integrate with customer vaults via connectors.
04:52 Sofia Rivera: From a product POV, can we get structured outputs to feed directly into our analytics pipeline? We want deterministic columns.
04:59 Priya Shah: That's the common use case - the structured JSON can be validated and then forwarded to your ingestion endpoint via function call. The Console's sink connector supports Kafka, S3, and webhooks.
05:12 Priya Shah: Switching to Console - here is the Optimize tab. For a given route we show batching suggestions, quantization recommendations, and model variant suggestions based on your throughput and sequence length.
05:24 Priya Shah: For Orion's invoice workload, we saw many short sequences - Optimize suggests smaller batch sizes with aggressive KV caching and a mid-tier quantized model to hit sub-100ms p95 while keeping cost 3x lower than full fp16.
05:41 Liam Chen: Do you have benchmarks or sample numbers we can run? We're currently on OpenAI and want to compare latency/cost.
05:48 Alex Carter: We'll run a pilot benchmark on your prompts. Typically we provide a script to run locally or via a Redwood-managed job - results come back with token-level cost, p50/p95, and resource consumption. We'll include that script in the follow-up.
06:03 Priya Shah: Demo: I trigger a sample benchmark which runs 1000 short invoice parses across a dedicated worker - results show 65ms median, 120ms p95, and cost per 1k tokens is X (demo placeholder).
06:18 Maya Thompson: That's promising. For us p95 under 200ms is a must. Also, our data residency requirement is EU-only.
06:26 Alex Carter: For data residency we can pin routing to EU regions and for Private deployments you can host in your VPC. We'll note EU-region Dedicated pricing separately.
06:37 Liam Chen: On the schema enforcement, what happens when the model invents a field or renames keys?
06:44 Priya Shah: The validator flags unknown fields as warnings or errors depending on your route policy. You can configure unknown field handling: drop, allow as extra_data, or block. We usually recommend drop + log for strict pipelines.
06:59 Maya Thompson: We're also worried about hallucinated values - e.g., model invents an invoice_id. Any suggestions?
07:06 Priya Shah: You can include a plausibility check step - e.g., cross-reference vendor names against a known vendor list (a secondary lookup), or add an optional human-in-the-loop approval for low-confidence extractions. The Console surfaces confidence scores per field.
07:20 Evan Park: Security specifics - does Redwood store KV cache content? Could that leak PII?
07:26 Alex Carter: KV cache is stored ephemeral by default and can be disabled. For Private deployments you control KV persistence and encryption. We'll include the optional KV encryption config in the docs.
07:38 Priya Shah: Now I'll show a slightly more advanced flow: multi-tool orchestration. The model extracts invoice info, calls verifyVendor(tool), which hits your internal vendor verification service, then calls postInvoice(tool) only if verified. You'll see function call payloads and conditional execution in the trace.
07:59 (brief pause, typing)
08:10 Priya Shah: (demo) Here's the trace: model -> verifyVendor(args) -> vendor returns trusted:true -> model then emits postInvoice(args). The Console trace timestamps each call and shows latency and errors.
08:29 Liam Chen: Nice. That trace is exactly what ops wants. Does the trace include model token logs?
08:35 Priya Shah: We record model inputs/outputs but you can redact token-level content; we keep the structured arguments and execution metadata by default. Audit retention is configurable per account.
08:49 Maya Thompson: On the ops side, we need metrics forwarded to our Datadog.
08:53 Priya Shah: We have exporters: Datadog, Prometheus, and file-based logs you can ship.
09:01 (interruption, coffee cup clink)
09:10 Priya Shah: Next - demo of schema-first development. You can author JSON schemas in the Console, test them in the playground, then export them as route templates. This makes rollout predictable across Hosted and Dedicated.
09:25 Sofia Rivera: Do you have versioning for schemas? We need rolling changes and canarying.
09:30 Priya Shah: Yes - schemas are versioned and you can do canary rollouts per-route. The Console supports A/B rollouts and automatic fallback to prior schema if error rate increases.
09:44 Alex Carter: Quick product note - our Smart Router can fallback to a cheaper model variant if Dedicated pool is saturated, and you can set guardrail policies per-customer.
09:55 Liam Chen: If fallback triggers, is the schema still enforced?
10:00 Priya Shah: Yes, enforcement is always applied at the route level. Fallback only changes the model variant; the runtime still validates the output. If the fallback model produces repeated failures, you can configure automatic rollbacks.
10:15 Maya Thompson: Pricing question - do you bill per token for structured output too?
10:20 Alex Carter: Yes, token-based billing for Hosted API. For Dedicated it's based on reserved capacity (GPU-hours) and a per-request multiplier for large seqs. We'll include sample pricing and a Dedicated proposal in the follow-up.
10:34 Evan Park: For legal/procurement, what SLAs and support tiers exist?
10:39 Alex Carter: We have Bronze/Silver/Gold enterprise tiers; Dedicated gets a 99.9% uptime SLA and enterprise support. Private is licensed. We'll include the SLA doc.
10:50 Priya Shah: Now I want to simulate an edge case: model returns malformed JSON and the repair loop doesn't fix it. You'll see the Console surface the raw output and a flagged action item for human review.
11:04 (demo shows raw text with missing bracket)
11:12 Priya Shah: In this case, route policy was set to require manual review for failures, so the tool call does not execute. An operator can either accept the repair or correct it.
11:27 Maya Thompson: That's useful. For us that manual gate will be for invoices > $100k.
11:33 Priya Shah: You can set conditional rules based on field values - amount thresholds, vendor risk score - all supported in the route policy engine.
11:45 Liam Chen: Switching topics a bit - latency. If we push to a dedicated pool in eu-west with 4x A100-ish instances, what p95 can we expect for short invoices?
11:56 Alex Carter: For short sequences on optimized kernels and batching disabled for low latency, we've seen p95 under 200ms. Optimize will give you per-deployment estimates based on model and sequence length distribution.
12:09 Liam Chen: Ok. Also, about model control - we want to run a specific open model with quantization. Is that supported?
12:16 Priya Shah: Yes, we curate model catalog with verified profiles, and you can bring your own model in Private. We support int8 and int4 quantized variants and our compiler picks kernels. Optimize will recommend quantization profile per workload.
12:29 Maya Thompson: Any concerns about quality regressions with quantized models?
12:33 Priya Shah: Slightly, so we recommend running a quality eval suite (we can run it for you) and monitor quality metrics in Console; Optimize ties regressions to prompt sets and triggers alerts.
12:46 Alex Carter: Time check - about 30 minutes in. Are there any specific things you want us to demo next?
12:52 Maya Thompson: I'd like to see the developer experience - SDK example showing schema enforcement and function calling.
12:58 Priya Shah: Sure. (typing) Here's a Python snippet using the SDK: create route with schema, call client.generate(schema=invoice_schema, mode='json'), handle function_call response; the SDK returns typed objects or raises ValidationError.
13:16 Liam Chen: Is the SDK open source? We want to fork if needed.
13:20 Alex Carter: SDKs are on GitHub; we welcome forks but please coordinate for enterprise support.
13:27 Sofia Rivera: Can we add a custom step that calls our fraud microservice as part of the pipeline?
13:32 Priya Shah: Absolutely - the tool registry supports internal services behind a VPC connector; calls can be executed in your network for Private deployments or via short-lived credentials for Dedicated.
13:44 Evan Park: About compliance again - do you have pen-test reports?
13:49 Alex Carter: We have a summary pen-test report and can share redacted results under NDA. We'll include that in the security packet.
13:56 (brief silence)
14:05 Priya Shah: Demo end-to-end: extraction -> verifyVendor -> fraudCheck -> postInvoice. Everything shows in a single trace with timestamps, call outcomes, and schema validation status.
14:22 Maya Thompson: That makes it easy to map into our downstream pipelines.
14:27 Liam Chen: A couple of nitty-gritty questions - can we set timeouts per function call?
14:32 Priya Shah: Yes, function/tool timeout and retry policy is configurable per registered tool. Timeouts are enforced by the runtime.
14:42 Maya Thompson: For the pilot, what would success metrics look like? We suggested: p95 < 200ms, schema pass rate > 98%, and cost <= current baseline.
14:52 Alex Carter: Perfect. We'll design the pilot to measure those exact metrics.
15:00 Priya Shah: Ok we'll close with an ask: please share a sample of 1k invoice images or parsed texts, your throughput targets, and any PII constraints; we'll run a 2-week pilot and return a benchmark report.
15:12 Maya Thompson: Timeline - procurement wants to get pricing this month.
15:16 Alex Carter: We'll prioritize pricing + Dedicated proposal and security packet.
15:20 Evan Park: Also include contract language for data residency and indemnities.
15:24 Alex Carter: Noted.
15:28 Priya Shah: Any final questions?
15:30 (short crosstalk)
15:34 Maya Thompson: No, thanks - that was thorough.
15:37 Alex Carter: Great. Recap of next steps: pricing + SOC2 docs + demo repo + benchmark script. We'll follow up with dates. Thanks everyone.
15:50 (meeting ends)
